name: Wendy Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What do you do in the factory?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a machine that prints labels on rolls for jars and cartons. I load ink and film, line up the marks and check that the colours stay in register. I am 58 and still junior on this press; I spent most of my working life in a family shop and learned this machine only recently. I finished secondary school, and I earn the usual operator pay.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and how do you handle unfamiliar tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Tomas repairs bicycles, and our two grown children have moved out. We have about five months of expenses saved and still pay for the house roof loan. A few other printing and packing plants are within reach, but their openings and pay vary. I use AI now and then to explain an unfamiliar ink term, then ask the senior printer before changing a mix. I like a proven method and learning beside somebody who has used it. We would like to stop full shifts one day, though we have not worked out whether the household figures allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the print room that faster order paperwork still needs a person to check the colour marks. A jar label with the wrong colour is a wasted run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas and I meet our present bills, and five months saved gives us some room. I need more practice on the press, but a slow change would let me finish learning this trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking the first labels against the colour sample and ask the senior printer before changing ink. I would use an AI explanation only alongside the printed mix sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly calm. The machine work stays recognisable, and I have somebody experienced to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error takes the longest to repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A faint second colour can be hard to see on a single label. I hold a whole printed roll beside the approved sample before signing the batch. Fixing the ink mix early saves the next pallet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask AI to choose an ink mix?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I might ask what a word means, but I use the approved mix sheet and the senior printer for actual quantities. My phone is not a colour standard.

say: I would **keep** physical colour checks even if order paperwork speeds up.
A **wrong** jar label wastes a whole print run.
think: **Present** household earnings pay bills and five months saved gives some room.
I **still** need practice on the label press.
do: **Keep** comparing first labels with the approved colour sample.
**Check** AI term explanations against printed ink sheets and senior advice.
feel: **Mostly** calm about familiar checks and continued paid practice.
S0.quote: I hold a whole printed roll beside the approved sample before signing the batch.
fieldNote: **Wendy** is a junior label-press operator learning colour registration after years in a family shop.
Her **typical** wage and bicycle-repairer husband Tomas cover bills, with five months saved and a roof loan remaining.
She **uses** AI occasionally for terms, but proven printed mixes and senior instruction govern machine settings.

steps.text: Keep comparing first printed rolls with approved colour sample

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the press crew office software may make orders faster before robots handle the ink and rolls. I would ask management to show the proposed shift changes before moving anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot loader could eventually leave fewer people tending the label press. I am still junior and would be easier to replace than the senior printer. Five months saved helps us wait, but it cannot cover a long cut to my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to watch a guarded full-roll robot trial and compare misprints with our current count. I would request an offered paid supervised training place before touching its controls. If a local print-checking vacancy is posted, I would apply only if its net pay after travel and its hours cover our roof loan and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the roster. I will learn a new control after someone proves it safe on our press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in the training place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A recognised class on paid hours, a fitter to show isolation and enough supervised time to practise safe stops. I would accept a funded place if it is actually offered and fits my shift. I would not call watching a robot trial the same as learning the controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no print-checking vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current press wage while checking posted operator work at the nearby plants. I would compare the pay after travel and the shift with our bills before applying. A plant nearby is not necessarily hiring.

say: I would **ask** for written shift changes and guarded print results.
**Office** order software comes before robot roll handling.
think: A **later** roll-loading robot could cut my junior label-press shifts.
**Five** months saved cannot carry a long wage cut.
do: **Request** guarded full-roll robot trial and compare misprints.
**Take** offered funded paid recognised training only with supervised isolation and workable hours.
**Apply** for posted checking work only with roof-loan-covering net pay and shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about junior roster risk, open to proven safe instruction.
S1.quote: I would not call watching a robot trial the same as learning the controls.
fieldNote: **Wendy** would observe a guarded trial, then train only if offered a funded paid recognised place with supervised safety practice.
Her **later** checking application requires a posting, sufficient net pay after travel and workable hours.
**Without** that vacancy she checks posted nearby operator work while keeping her current wage.

steps.text: Request guarded roll-handling trial and compare misprint counts
Take offered funded paid recognised class with supervised isolation and workable hours
Apply for posted print-checking job only with bill-covering net pay after travel and shift
Check posted operator jobs if no vacancy and net pay after travel and shift fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my neighbours AGI can plan orders in 2028, but capable robots loading, printing and checking labels around 2031 may take the factory shifts. I would ask for real notice before the second change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most junior label-press hours to disappear once robots can set the run and pull bad labels. I will be 63 then. Five months saved is helpful, but losing my wage while Tomas’s repair orders vary would leave the roof loan and heating bills exposed; I would lie awake over that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas and I would postpone replacing the car and list roof-loan, food and heating costs. I would ask the plant for written redeployment terms and ask our lender about payments before any instalment is missed. I would apply for a posted local print-inspection job only if paid safety training is offered and its net pay and hours cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about a large expected wage loss. I could still make the calls, but a reserve is not a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the grown children support you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They might help if they offered, but both have rent of their own. I would not put our roof loan on them. We have to work from income we can count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you keep setting ink after robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps during installation, but I would need a posted role and a safe paid training place before relying on that. I would not assume the senior printer’s job becomes mine. The plant must name the hours and pay.

say: I would **distinguish** 2028 order AGI from physical robot printing around 2031.
I would **seek** real notice and redeployment terms.
think: **Five** months saved cannot replace my wage against roof-loan and heating costs.
do: **Postpone** car replacement and list essential bills.
**Ask** plant for redeployment terms and lender about payment options.
**Apply** for posted inspection work only with paid safe training and bill-covering net wages and hours.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and awake over household bills.
S2.quote: I would not assume the senior printer’s job becomes mine.
fieldNote: **Wendy** expects hands-on robot displacement around 2031, about three years after AGI changes ordering.
A **five-month** reserve and several local plants do not erase risk to her wage and roof loan.
An **inspection** application requires an actual local posting, paid safety instruction and enough net pay and hours for bills.

steps.text: Postpone planned car replacement and list roof-loan and heating costs
Ask plant for written redeployment terms
Ask lender about payment options before missed instalment
Apply for posted inspection work only with paid safety training and bill-covering net pay and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the plant five years is time to arrange a real apprenticeship for people still learning the press. AGI changes orders in 2031 and capable robots reach the print line around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 66 by the robot date. A new control is possible for me after proper practice, but I do not know safe isolation yet. Our hoped-for retirement cannot be assumed while the roof loan remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would accept an offered recognised print-maintenance course only if funded on paid shifts with supervised robot isolation and class hours I can attend. After qualifying, I would apply for a posted local print-checking or maintenance role only if net pay after travel and hours cover our bills. If no safe paid place opens, I would keep the press wage and search posted nearby print jobs with suitable pay and shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real place opening in time. Five years helps if somebody teaches me safely while I am paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe practice include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter would show me the lockout, then watch me prove the print robot cannot move before opening a guard. I would repeat that on paid time until the assessment is passed. A short tour would not be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire instead of taking a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Tomas and I have written income figures that cover the roof loan and living costs. We have not checked that yet. I cannot pay the heating bill merely by turning 66.

say: I would **ask** for a paid recognised apprenticeship before 2034 robots.
**AGI** order changes come in 2031, ahead of physical printing robots.
think: At 66, **retirement** depends on real household income and roof-loan figures.
I **need** supervised robot isolation before any maintenance job.
do: **Take** offered funded paid recognised course with supervised isolation and attendable hours.
**Apply** after qualification for posted print role only with bill-covering net pay and shifts.
If **no** safe paid place, seek posted nearby print jobs with suitable wage and hours.
feel: **Anxious** about course availability, willing to learn with safe paid practice.
S3.quote: I cannot pay the heating bill merely by turning 66.
fieldNote: **Wendy** would take an offered recognised funded paid course with supervised lockout and attendable hours.
**After** qualifying she separately applies for a posted role only at net pay and hours that cover bills.
**Without** a safe paid place she retains the press wage and checks posted nearby print jobs.

steps.text: Take offered recognised funded paid course with supervised robot isolation and class hours
Apply for posted print job only with bill-covering net pay after travel and workable shifts
Seek posted nearby print work if no course and wage and hours fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my family ten years is long enough to price retirement honestly and train anybody who still needs the factory wage. AGI changes orders in 2036 and capable robots reach the press around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 when orders change and 71 when robots arrive. I might have stopped full shifts by then, but Tomas and I have not calculated what the roof loan and living costs require. I cannot promise either retirement or work at 71 based on the roof-loan figures we have today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written retirement-income and cost estimates this year. If they show I still need paid work, I would take an offered recognised funded course on paid shifts with supervised robot isolation, then apply for a posted local print role only if net pay and hours meet our bills. Without a safe paid place, I would search posted print or packing work at viable wages and shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the figures we do not yet have. Time to plan helps, but it cannot promise a training place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children take over the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They can visit and advise us, but their own households come first. Tomas and I need to see the actual monthly income and roof payment. We should not call family kindness a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach before leaving the press?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach how to compare a full label roll with the approved colour sample. Even if a robot loads it, the customer still sees the wrong shade. I can pass on that check while I am working.

say: I would **ask** for retirement figures and paid training for those still working.
think: At 68 in 2036, I **may** have left full shifts if income permits.
At 71 **near** 2039, factory work depends on actual household costs.
do: **Request** written retirement income and household cost figures.
If **work** is needed, take offered funded paid safe course on attendable shifts.
**After** qualification, apply for posted print work only with bill-covering net pay and hours.
feel: **Uneasy** about unknown retirement figures and future course availability.
S4.quote: I cannot promise either retirement or work at 71 based on the roof-loan figures we have today.
fieldNote: **Wendy** does not assume a pension or continued employment at the 2039 robot date.
If **still** earning, her course needs an offered funded paid place with supervised safety and workable hours.
A **separate** posted job needs enough net pay; without a course she checks posted print or packing work.

steps.text: Request written retirement income and cost figures

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because robots could remove junior label-press hours around 2031 while the roof loan remains. An offered paid safety apprenticeship and a posted job with enough net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: My grown children can advise, but they cannot be the plan for paying our roof loan. I hold a whole printed roll beside the approved sample before signing the batch.

headlineQuote: My grown children can advise, but they cannot be the plan for paying our roof loan.
portrait: **Wendy** Reyes, 58, is a junior label-press operator with secondary schooling and typical machine pay.
She and **bicycle-repairer** husband Tomas have grown children, a roof loan and about five months saved.
She **uses** AI occasionally for ink terms but relies on proven printed mixes and experienced operator advice.
**Several** nearby plants offer possibilities, while anticipated robot cuts and uncertain retirement income still worry her.
She **favours** earned work and practical apprenticeship, with paid safe training and posted jobs subject to viable net pay.
biggestWorry: **Capable** robots around 2031 could remove her junior label-press hours while the roof loan remains.
whatWouldHelp: **Offer** funded paid supervised training and posted local work whose net wage and hours cover bills.
